fig14_1: Two side-by-side panels for a clamped beam under an exponential load solved by the polynomial trick. The left panel plots beam deflection versus position x from minus one to one; open circles for the N equals sixteen numerical solution sit exactly on the solid exact-solution curve, which dips into a small, asymmetric well skewed toward one side. The right panel uses two log scales: maximum error (left axis, solid) falls geometrically with N, reaching about five times ten to the power minus sixteen near N equals fifteen, while the condition number of the interior operator (right axis, dashed) rises like N to the eighth power, the eventual accuracy limiter.
fig14_2: Two panels characterising clamped-beam eigenmodes at N equals twenty. The left panel overlays the first six mode shapes (normalised to unit maximum) versus position, alternating between symmetric single-hump shapes and antisymmetric shapes with a sign change at the centre, each vanishing with zero slope at both walls. The right panel is a semilog plot of relative eigenvalue error versus mode number: the error stays near machine precision for low modes then climbs sharply, so only the first roughly two-thirds N eigenvalues are accurate.
fig14_3: Two log-scale panels comparing the direct polynomial-trick method against the coupled second-order reformulation for the clamped beam. The left panel plots maximum error versus N for both methods; both fall geometrically (spectral convergence), but the coupled method keeps falling and holds low error to larger N while the direct method bottoms out and degrades sooner. The right panel plots condition number versus N on log-log axes, with the direct curve rising as N to the eighth power and the coupled curve as N to the fourth power, confirming the conditioning advantage.
fig14_4: Two panels for the two-dimensional biharmonic boundary value problem with a manufactured solution. The left panel is a filled contour plot over the square from minus one to one in x and y of the numerical solution at N equals twenty-four, a smooth non-negative hump that vanishes on all edges and peaks at the four interior points where x and y equal plus or minus one half. The right panel is a semilog plot of maximum error versus N: the error drops exponentially until about N equals twenty to twenty-two, then plateaus near ten to the power minus twelve as the N to the eighth power conditioning of the biharmonic operator takes over.
fig14_5: A five-by-five grid of twenty-five small contour plots showing the first twenty-five eigenmodes of a clamped square plate, ordered by increasing eigenvalue. Each panel displays the nodal-line pattern where the mode is zero: the first is a single central dome, and successive modes develop progressively more nodal lines and intricate cellular patterns. Several pairs of panels look identical apart from a ninety-degree rotation, marking degenerate eigenvalue pairs produced by the square symmetry of the domain, such as the second and third modes.
fig14_6: A four-by-three grid of twelve small contour plots showing the first twelve even-even eigenmodes of the clamped square plate, computed on the quarter domain and ordered by increasing eigenvalue. Each pattern is mirror-symmetric about both the x equals zero and y equals zero axes, with increasingly many nodal lines for higher modes. These quarter-domain eigenvalues match the full-domain computation to full numerical precision, illustrating exact symmetry reduction.
fig14_7: A two-by-two grid of complex-plane scatter plots of the Orr-Sommerfeld spectrum for plane Poiseuille flow at wavenumber alpha equals one and Reynolds number five thousand seven hundred seventy-two, computed with forty, sixty, eighty, and one hundred Chebyshev points. Each panel plots eigenvalues c with real phase speed on the horizontal axis and imaginary part on the vertical axis; the horizontal line at imaginary part zero divides stable (below) from unstable (above). The points trace a characteristic Y-shaped pattern of three branches whose core is identical across panels while the branch tips shift with resolution. One rightmost eigenvalue near phase speed zero point two-four sits just barely above the line, marking marginal instability.
fig14_8: A complex-plane contour plot of the epsilon-pseudospectra of the non-normal Orr-Sommerfeld operator at N equals one hundred, Reynolds number five thousand seven hundred seventy-two, wavenumber one. Dots mark the eigenvalues, all lying in the stable lower half-plane (imaginary part of c below zero), while nested level curves for epsilon equal to ten to the power minus two, minus four, minus six, minus eight, and minus ten surround them. The outer contours balloon upward across the imaginary-part-zero stability boundary into the unstable region, showing that a perturbation as small as about ten to the power minus four can make an eigenvalue unstable, the non-normality mechanism behind subcritical transition.
fig14_9: A space-time plot of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky solution on the interval zero to thirty-two pi, with N equals two hundred fifty-six modes integrated by ETDRK4 to time one hundred fifty. Position runs along one axis and time along the other, with solution amplitude shown as colour. After a brief transient up to about time twenty in which long-wavelength stripes emerge, the field settles into sustained spatiotemporal chaos: diagonal cellular streaks that continually merge, split, and weave without ever forming a steady or periodic pattern.
tbl14_1: A summary table listing the nine computational etudes of the chapter, giving for each its number, the problem solved (from the clamped beam and biharmonic plate to Orr-Sommerfeld stability and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky chaos), the key spectral technique used, and a one-line highlight such as the N to the fourth versus N to the eighth conditioning trade-off and the critical Reynolds number near five thousand seven hundred seventy-two.
